questions.prompt: What does `git diff` (with no arguments) show?

options.text: The changes between the last two commits
Your unstaged changes: the working tree vs. the staging area
Everything that has ever changed in the repo
The differences between your branch and the remote

questions.explanation: Bare `git diff` compares the working tree to the staging area — i.e. the changes you have made but not yet staged.

questions.prompt: Which command shows exactly what your next commit will contain?
questions.explanation: git diff --staged (also --cached) compares the staging area to the last commit, showing precisely the changes that are about to be committed.

questions.prompt: Which statements about .gitignore are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: It lists patterns of files Git should not track
It supports glob patterns like *.log and build/
It only affects files that are currently untracked
It automatically untracks files you already committed

questions.explanation: gitignore holds glob patterns for untracked files and only prevents tracking of files not already committed. Removing an already-tracked file needs git rm --cached.

questions.prompt: To view history with one compact line per commit, run: git log --______
questions.explanation: git log --oneline prints each commit as a short hash plus its subject line — a quick overview, often paired with --graph.

questions.prompt: You added `secrets.env` to .gitignore, but Git still tracks it. Why?

options.text: The file was already committed; .gitignore doesn't untrack existing files
You need to restart Git for .gitignore to take effect

questions.explanation: .gitignore only stops Git from tracking currently-untracked files. A file that was already committed keeps being tracked until you git rm --cached it.

questions.prompt: Match each `git log` option to what it shows.

pairs.right: An ASCII graph of branches and merges
The full diff for each commit

questions.explanation: --oneline compresses each commit to a line, --graph draws branch topology, --stat summarizes changed files, and -p shows the patches.
